what: IREN builds and runs large data centres powered largely by renewable electricity. It began mining bitcoin and is converting much of its capacity to artificial-intelligence computing, renting out graphics processors and building facilities for AI customers in Texas, British Columbia and elsewhere.
customers: On the mining side there is no customer. On the computing side, AI companies renting graphics processing capacity by the hour, and larger customers contracting whole facilities.
money: Bitcoin earned from running mining machines on owned sites.
Renting out graphics processors, and building and operating data centre capacity for AI customers.
moat: IREN owns land, power contracts and grid connections at sites it developed itself, which is the genuinely scarce input in AI computing: electricity that can be delivered at scale, with permits already in hand. Having built the facilities rather than bought them also means it knows how to build the next ones, which is a real operating advantage when everyone is trying to build at once.
risks: The trailing twelve months show a net loss of about $1.4B and free cash flow of roughly negative $2.5B. This is an enormous construction programme, not a profitable business.
Debt has risen to about $7.6B. Cash of $5.9B covers much of it today, but the spending continues and the financing terms matter enormously.
The shares trade at about 8.8 times sales while deeply loss-making.
Nineteen analysts average a $56.69 target against a $14.41 price — nearly 300% above. A gap that size is not a forecast; it is a disagreement about whether this works at all.
Graphics processors depreciate quickly and their rental price falls as supply arrives. Capacity bought at today’s prices has to earn back before that happens.
opportunities: Revenue has grown extraordinarily, from $187.2M in 2024 to $707.0M in 2026, with trailing revenue of about $694.7M.
Renewable-powered sites with secured grid connections are exactly what AI computing needs and cannot easily obtain.
Moving from mining to AI computing raises revenue per megawatt several times over and replaces bitcoin exposure with customer contracts.
Cash of $5.9B gives it the means to keep building through a period when smaller competitors cannot raise money.
watch: Contracted AI revenue as a share of the total, and the terms of the next financing. The construction is visible; whether it is paid for by customers or by shareholders is what decides the outcome.
view: Start with the scale of what is happening here, because the numbers are easy to misread. IREN lost $1.4 billion and consumed $2.5 billion of cash over the trailing year, and it holds $5.9 billion of cash against $7.6 billion of debt. That is not a company in trouble; it is a company in the middle of an enormous construction programme, funded in advance. The income statement describes the building phase, not the business. Whether this is a good investment depends entirely on what the finished buildings earn and who has agreed to pay for them.

The asset is real and it is the right one. The binding constraint on AI computing is not chips, which are being manufactured as fast as the fabs allow, but electricity: land with a grid connection, power contracts and permits, at a scale measured in hundreds of megawatts. IREN developed its own sites rather than buying them, which means it holds that scarce input and knows how to build the next one. Revenue going from $187 million to over $700 million in two years says the conversion from mining to computing is actually happening rather than being announced.

Now the part that should give anyone pause. Nineteen analysts average $56.69 against a $14.41 share price — nearly 300% upside. A spread like that is not a consensus forecast; it is the market and the analysts disagreeing about whether the business model works, and the market is the one with money at risk. The specific worry is sound: graphics processors depreciate fast and their rental price falls as supply arrives, so capacity bought at today’s prices must earn back within a few years. If the contracts behind it are long and the customers are creditworthy, the maths works. If the revenue is hourly rentals at spot prices, it may not.

So the question I would put to this company is narrow and answerable: what share of the AI revenue is contracted, for how long, and with whom. That single disclosure separates a data centre business from a speculative compute rental operation, and the valuation that follows is wildly different. Until it is answered clearly, this is a position to size as the binary it is, and to judge on financing terms rather than on revenue growth, which at this stage proves only that money is being spent.
bull: The sites convert to contracted AI capacity with creditworthy customers on long terms, revenue per megawatt multiplies, and the scarce asset is power that nobody else can get.
bear: The revenue turns out to be short-term GPU rental into a market where supply is arriving fast, the processors depreciate before they pay back, and $7.6 billion of debt meets falling prices.
